text: Because it is relatively cheap thioacetazone has been used in some countries with limited resources but its use is strongly discour- aged because of its weak antimycobacterial activity and associated risk of fatal skin toxicity, particularly in HIV patients. All first-line drugs can be given intermittently (at double doses 3 times each week) as an alternative to daily use. Patients who remain smear-positive at the end of supervised short-course chemotherapy may have drug-resistant tuberculosis and treatment usually re- quires the introduction of second-line drugs (see below). First-line drugs such as isoniazid, rifampicin, and particu- larly pyrazinamide may cause severe and possibly fatal drug-induced hepatitis. Further details covering hepato- toxicity and special precautions for use in patients with liv- er disorders are given in the respective drug mono- graphs—see, Isoniazid p.289; Rifampicin p.326; and Pyrazinamide p.320. UK4 and US5 guidelines recommend stopping all potentially hepatotoxic drugs if serum transaminases rise to more than 5 times the upper limit of normal or 3 times in the presence of symptoms of hepatitis or elevated bilirubin. Cautious sequential re-introduction of the same drugs (with or without pyrazinamide) after res- olution of the biochemical abnormalities is often possi- ble.4-6 Patients in whom therapy is interrupted may be giv- en streptomycin, ethambutol, and/or a fluoroquinolone until hepatotoxicity has resolved. Management of drug-resistant disease. The incidence of drug resistance amongst M. tuberculosis strains has in- creased over recent years typically in countries with poor tuberculosis control programmes.8,9 Isoniazid and strepto- mycin resistance are the most prevalent. Multidrug-resist- ant tuberculosis (caused by strains resistant to both isoni- azid and rifampicin) requires a combination of first- and second-line drugs for at least 18 to 24 months (see be- low).4,5,8 Drug-resistant tuberculosis is a reflection of poor tuberculosis management, control, and unreliable drug supply; it is difficult to treat, and not infrequently fatal, particularly in HIV-infected patients. Whereas the WHO DOTS programme may limit the development of multi- drug-resistant tuberculosis, different strategies are re- quired in areas where multidrug resistance is already es- tablished. These have been formulated by the WHO in the DOTS-plus strategy for countries with well functioning tuberculosis control programmes.10 Patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis and those who relapse after completing the WHO standard treatment regimens should receive a DOTS-plus regimen, which in- cludes second-line antituberculous drugs.
